Every question on this sheet is a **real past-paper question** — Sections A–B from TMUA Paper 2, Section C
from the MAT (source given under each). For each, decide whether the argument is correct, or find the
**first** step/line that is wrong. Read line by line and ask: *"does this follow, for every value the
previous line allows?"*

---

## Section A — Which step is invalid?

**A1.** &nbsp; Consider the following problem: *Solve the inequality
$\left(\dfrac14\right)^{n}<\left(\dfrac1{32}\right)^{10}$, where $n$ is a positive integer.*

A student produces the following argument:

$$\left(\tfrac14\right)^{n}<\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10} \qquad\text{— then step (I) gives —}$$
$$\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac14\right)^{n}<\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)^{10} \qquad\text{— (II) —}$$
$$n\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac14\right)<10\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac1{32}\right) \qquad\text{— (III) —}$$
$$n<\frac{10\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac1{32}\right)}{\log_{\frac12}\left(\tfrac14\right)} \qquad\text{— (IV) —}$$
$$n<\frac{10\times5}{2}=25 \qquad\text{— (V) —}$$
$$1\leq n\leq 24$$

Which step (if any) in the argument is invalid? &nbsp; **A** none; the argument is correct &nbsp;
**B** only (I) &nbsp; **C** only (II) &nbsp; **D** only (III) &nbsp; **E** only (IV) &nbsp; **F** only (V)

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Answer + reason:
:::

**A2.** &nbsp; Consider the following attempt to solve the equation $4x\sqrt{2x-1}=10x-5$:

$$4x\sqrt{2x-1}=10x-5 \qquad\text{— (I) —}$$
$$4x\sqrt{2x-1}=5(2x-1) \qquad\text{— (II) —}$$
$$16x^{2}(2x-1)=25(2x-1)^{2} \qquad\text{— (III) —}$$
$$16x^{2}=25(2x-1) \qquad\text{— (IV) —}$$
$$16x^{2}-50x+25=0 \qquad\text{— (V) —}$$
$$(8x-5)(2x-5)=0 \qquad\text{— (VI) —}$$
$$\text{The solutions of the original equation are } x=\tfrac58 \text{ and } x=\tfrac52.$$

Which one of the following is true? &nbsp; **A** The solution is correct. &nbsp; **B** Only one of
$x=\tfrac58,\tfrac52$ is correct and the error arises from step (II). &nbsp; **C** …from step (III).
&nbsp; **D** …from step (IV). &nbsp; **E** There is another value of $x$ that satisfies the original
equation and the error arises from step (II). &nbsp; **F** …from step (III). &nbsp; **G** …from step
(IV).

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Answer + reason:
:::

## Section B — Evaluate the proof

**B1.** &nbsp; The following is an attempted proof of the conjecture: **if $\tan\theta>0$, then
$\sin\theta+\cos\theta>1$.**

Suppose $\tan\theta>0$, so in particular $\cos\theta\neq0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)** &nbsp; Since $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, then
$\sin\theta\cos\theta=\tan\theta\cos^{2}\theta>0$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)** &nbsp; It follows that $1+2\sin\theta\cos\theta>1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)** &nbsp; Therefore $\sin^{2}\theta+2\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos^{2}\theta>1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)** &nbsp; which factorises to give $(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}>1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)** &nbsp; Therefore $\sin\theta+\cos\theta>1$.

Which one of the following is the case? &nbsp; **A** The proof is correct. &nbsp; **B** First error in
line (I). &nbsp; **C** line (II). &nbsp; **D** line (III). &nbsp; **E** line (IV). &nbsp; **F** line (V).

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Answer + reason:
:::

**B2.** &nbsp; Consider the following claim: *The difference between two consecutive positive cube numbers
is always prime.* Here is an attempted proof:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $(x+1)^{3}=x^{3}+3x^{2}+3x+1$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; Taking $x$ to be a positive integer, the difference between two consecutive cube
numbers can be expressed as $(x+1)^{3}-x^{3}=3x^{2}+3x+1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; It is impossible to factorise $3x^{2}+3x+1$ into two linear factors with integer
coefficients because its discriminant is negative.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; Therefore for every positive integer value of $x$ the integer $3x^{2}+3x+1$
cannot be factorised.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; Hence, the difference between two consecutive cube numbers will always be prime.

Which of the following best describes this proof? &nbsp; **A** completely correct, claim true. &nbsp;
**B** completely correct, but there are counterexamples to the claim. &nbsp; **C** wrong, first error line
I. &nbsp; **D** line II. &nbsp; **E** line III. &nbsp; **F** line IV. &nbsp; **G** line V.

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Answer + reason:
:::

**B3.** &nbsp; A student attempts to answer: *What is the largest number of consecutive odd integers that
are all prime?* The attempt is as follows:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; There are two consecutive odd integers that are prime (for example: $17,19$).
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; Any three consecutive odd integers can be written in the form $n-2,\,n,\,n+2$
for some $n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; If $n$ is one more than a multiple of $3$, then $n+2$ is a multiple of $3$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; If $n$ is two more than a multiple of $3$, then $n-2$ is a multiple of $3$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; The only other possibility is that $n$ is a multiple of $3$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI** &nbsp; In each case, one of the integers is a multiple of $3$, so not prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**VII** &nbsp; Therefore the largest number of consecutive odd integers that are all prime is two.

Which of the following best describes this attempt? &nbsp; **A** completely correct. &nbsp; **B** first
error line I. &nbsp; **C** line II. &nbsp; **D** line III. &nbsp; **E** line IV. &nbsp; **F** line V.
&nbsp; **G** line VI. &nbsp; **H** line VII.

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Answer + reason:
:::

**B4.** &nbsp; A student is asked to prove whether the following statement $(*)$ is true or false:

$$(*)\quad\text{For all real numbers } a \text{ and } b,\ \ |a+b|<|a|+|b|.$$

The student's proof is as follows: *Statement $(*)$ is **false**. A counterexample is $a=3,\,b=4$, as
$|3+4|=7$ and $|3|+|4|=7$, but $7<7$ is false.*

Which of the following best describes the student's proof? &nbsp; **A** $(*)$ is true, and the proof is
not correct. &nbsp; **B** $(*)$ is false, but the proof is not correct: the counterexample is not valid.
&nbsp; **C** $(*)$ is false, but the proof is not correct: the student needs to give *all* the values of
$a,b$ where $|a+b|<|a|+|b|$ is false. &nbsp; **D** $(*)$ is false, but the proof is not correct: the
student should have stated $|a+b|\leq|a|+|b|$. &nbsp; **E** $(*)$ is false, and the proof is fully
correct.

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Answer + reason:
:::

## Section C — Cross-exam (MAT)

**C1.** &nbsp; For all real $n$, it is the case that
$n^{4}+1=\left(n^{2}+\sqrt2\,n+1\right)\left(n^{2}-\sqrt2\,n+1\right)$. From this we may deduce that
$n^{4}+4$ is

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** never a prime number for any positive whole number $n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** a prime number for exactly one positive whole number $n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** a prime number for exactly two positive whole numbers $n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** a prime number for exactly three positive whole numbers $n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(e)** a prime number for exactly four positive whole numbers $n$.

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3.5cm"}
Answer + reason:
:::
